Describing a box

Four numbers, three conventions, many bugs

Act 2 · Describing a box · Day 2 · 15 / 121

2.15 · section

Floor content, but it causes real bugs in production.

Act 2 · Describing a box

A bounding box

Bounding box — the smallest axis-aligned rectangle that contains an object, described by four numbers.
Act 2 · Describing a box · Day 2 · 16 / 121

2.16 · definition

Axis-aligned means the sides are horizontal and vertical. Rotated boxes exist for aerial images; we skip them.

Act 2 · Describing a box

Three box formats

xyxy(x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max)torchvision, Pascal VOC
xywh(x_min, y_min, width, height)COCO
cxcywh(x_centre, y_centre, width, height)YOLO, DETR — often normalised to 0–1
Act 2 · Describing a box · Day 2 · 17 / 121

2.17 · table

Same box, three ways of writing it. Mixing them up is silent — the box just lands in the wrong place.

Worked example

Converting formats — worked

  1. Image 640 × 480
  2. Box xyxy = (100, 120, 300, 360)
  3. xywh = (100, 120, 200, 240)
  4. cxcywh = (200, 240, 200, 240)
  5. normalised cxcywh = (0.3125, 0.5, 0.3125, 0.5)
Act 2 · Describing a box · Day 2 · 18 / 121

2.18 · worked

Width = 300 − 100, centre x = 100 + 200/2. Normalise by dividing x values by 640 and y values by 480.

Act 2 · Describing a box

Gotcha: normalised vs pixel coordinates

Normalised

  • values 0–1
  • independent of image size

Pixels

  • values up to width and height

A normalised box drawn as pixels is a tiny box in the top-left corner

Act 2 · Describing a box · Day 2 · 19 / 121

2.19 · compare

If all your boxes are crammed into the top-left corner, you forgot to multiply by the image size.

Act 2 · Describing a box

Comparing two boxes: IoU

IoU (Intersection over Union) — the area where two boxes overlap divided by the area they cover together. 0 = no overlap
  • 1 = identical.
Act 2 · Describing a box · Day 2 · 20 / 121

2.20 · definition

IoU is how detection decides whether a prediction "hit" the real object.

Worked example

IoU — worked example 1

  1. A = (0, 0, 4, 4) · area 16
  2. B = (2, 2, 6, 6) · area 16
  3. Intersection = (2, 2, 4, 4) · area 4
  4. Union = 16 + 16 − 4 = 28
  5. IoU = 4 / 28 ≈ 0.14
Act 2 · Describing a box · Day 2 · 21 / 121

2.21 · worked

The boxes look like they overlap a fair bit, but IoU is only 0.14. Intuition underestimates how strict IoU is.

Worked example

IoU — worked example 2

  1. A = (0, 0, 4, 4) · area 16
  2. B = (1, 0, 5, 4) · area 16
  3. Intersection = (1, 0, 4, 4) · area 12
  4. Union = 16 + 16 − 12 = 20
  5. IoU = 12 / 20 = 0.60
Act 2 · Describing a box · Day 2 · 22 / 121

2.22 · worked

Shifted by one unit out of four, IoU is 0.6. Identical boxes give 1.0.

Act 2 · Describing a box

What IoU values look like

010.3loosely on the object
020.5the classic "hit" threshold
030.75tight
040.9almost perfect
Act 2 · Describing a box · Day 2 · 23 / 121

2.23 · cards

IoU Darts will train your eye for these numbers.

Act 2 · Describing a box

IoU in code

ix1, iy1 = max(a.x1, b.x1), max(a.y1, b.y1)
ix2, iy2 = min(a.x2, b.x2), min(a.y2, b.y2)
inter = max(0, ix2 − ix1) * max(0, iy2 − iy1)
union = area(a) + area(b) − inter
iou = inter / union
Act 2 · Describing a box · Day 2 · 24 / 121

2.24 · code

The max(0, …) handles boxes that do not overlap at all. Forgetting it gives negative areas.

  • Closest team wins

03

Many objects: the two-stage story

First find places that might contain an object, then classify each one

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 28 / 121

2.28 · section

Each detector in this act fixes the slowness of the previous one.

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story

Idea 1: the sliding window

  • Repeat at many window sizes and shapes
Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 29 / 121

2.29 · diagram

It works in principle. Let's count the cost.

Worked example

Why sliding windows explode

  1. 640 × 480 image
  2. a window every 8 pixels → about 4,800 positions
  3. × 10 sizes × 3 shapes → about 144,000 crops
  4. each needs a CNN pass
  5. and most of them are background
Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 30 / 121

2.30 · worked

Far too slow. We need to look only where objects probably are.

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story

Idea 2: region proposals

Region proposal — a candidate box that might contain an object, found by a fast method that groups similar pixels (e.g. selective search). About 2,000 per image instead of 100,000+.
Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 31 / 121

2.31 · definition

Proposals do not know what the object is. They only say "something might be here".

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story

R-CNN (2014)

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 32 / 121

2.32 · diagram

R stands for regions. It was a big accuracy jump over hand-crafted features.

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story

R-CNN's problem

012,000 CNN passes per image
02about 47 seconds per image
03Overlapping regions recompute the same features again and again
04Three separate training stages
Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 33 / 121

2.33 · cards

Forty-seven seconds per image is not usable for video. Where is the waste?

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story

Fast R-CNN: compute features once

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 34 / 121

2.34 · diagram

Crop the features, not the pixels. One CNN pass instead of two thousand.

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story

RoI pooling

RoI pooling — take a region of the feature map of any size and pool it into a fixed grid (e.g. 7 × 7), so every proposal gives the same-sized input to the head.
Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 35 / 121

2.35 · definition

The head needs fixed-size input, but proposals come in all sizes. RoI pooling solves that.

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Fast R-CNN's new bottleneck

The CNN now takes a fraction of a second. The slow part is the proposal method — selective search runs on the CPU and takes about 2 seconds.

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 36 / 121

2.36 · rule

Fix one bottleneck and another appears. That is engineering.

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story

Faster R-CNN: the network proposes

  • Everything is one network, trained together
Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 37 / 121

2.37 · diagram

Let the network learn where objects are likely to be. This removed the last hand-designed step.

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story

Anchors

Anchor — a pre-defined template box placed at every feature-map position. The RPN predicts, for each anchor, "is there an object?" and how to nudge the anchor to fit it.
Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 38 / 121

2.38 · definition

Instead of predicting boxes from nothing, the network adjusts templates. Much easier to learn.

Worked example

Anchors — worked

  1. 3 scales (small, medium, large) × 3 aspect ratios (1:2, 1:1, 2:1) = 9 anchors per position
  2. Feature map 40 × 30 → 1,200 positions × 9 ≈ 10,800 anchors
  3. The RPN keeps the best few hundred
Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 39 / 121

2.39 · worked

Many anchors, few objects. That imbalance matters in training.

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story

The two-stage pattern

  • classify and refine: "what is it, exactly where?"
  • Accurate, especially for small objects
  • slower than one-stage
Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 40 / 121

2.40 · diagram

Faster R-CNN is still a strong, accurate baseline. Lab 2A runs it from torchvision.

Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story

The two-stage family

R-CNNCNN per proposal~47 s / image
Fast R-CNNCNN once, RoI pooling~2 s (proposals are slow)
Faster R-CNNlearned proposals (RPN)about 5–7 images / s on a 2015 GPU
Mask R-CNN+ a mask head (Act 7)
Act 3 · Many objects — the two-stage story · Day 2 · 41 / 121

2.41 · table

Read the middle column. Each row fixed the slow part of the row above it.

04

Scale and duplicates

Two problems every detector must solve

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · Day 2 · 42 / 121

2.42 · section

Small objects and duplicate boxes. Both cause most real-world failures.

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · The scale problem

A person close to the camera is 400 pixels tall. A person far away is 20 pixels tall. Same class, 20× size difference.

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · Day 2 · 43 / 121

2.43 · rule

Deep layers have a big receptive field — good for big objects, terrible for tiny ones.

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates

Fix 1: the image pyramid

Idea

  • run the detector on the image at several sizes (100%, 50%, 25%)

Cost

  • several full passes
  • accurate but slow
Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · Day 2 · 44 / 121

2.44 · compare

Works, but multiplies the cost.

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates

Fix 2: the Feature Pyramid Network

  • Early layers
  • high resolution, weak meaning
  • Deep layers
  • low resolution, strong meaning
  • FPN
  • pass deep meaning back up to the high-resolution layers → detect small objects on fine maps, large objects on coarse maps
Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · Day 2 · 45 / 121

2.45 · diagram

One pass, many scales. FPN is inside almost every modern detector, including the torchvision models we use.

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · The duplicate problem

A detector usually fires several overlapping boxes on the same object — all with high confidence. We want one box per object.

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · Day 2 · 46 / 121

2.46 · rule

Show a photo with five boxes stacked on one car.

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates

Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)

NMS — keep the highest-confidence box, delete every other box that overlaps it by more than an IoU threshold, then repeat with the next highest remaining box.
Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · Day 2 · 47 / 121

2.47 · definition

Keep the best, remove its copies, repeat.

Worked example

NMS step by step

  1. Boxes (score): A 0.95 · B 0.90 · C 0.80 · D 0.75 · E 0.60 · F 0.55
  2. IoU threshold 0.5
  3. Keep A → remove B (IoU 0.7 with A) and D (0.6)
  4. Next highest left: C → keep → remove E (0.65 with C)
  5. Next: F → keep (overlaps nothing above 0.5)
  6. Result: A, C, F
Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · Day 2 · 48 / 121

2.48 · worked

Walk through it slowly. Be NMS lets them do exactly this.

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates

The NMS threshold

Too high (0.9)

  • almost nothing is removed
  • duplicates survive

Too low (0.2)

  • real neighbouring objects get deleted

Typical: 0.45–0.7

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · Day 2 · 49 / 121

2.49 · compare

The threshold is a trade-off between duplicates and missed neighbours.

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates

Two knobs people confuse

Confidence threshold

  • "how sure must a box be to show at all?"
  • removes weak boxes

NMS IoU threshold

  • "how much overlap counts as a duplicate?"
  • removes copies
Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · Day 2 · 50 / 121

2.50 · compare

They do completely different jobs. Many bug reports are someone changing the wrong one.

Act 4 · Scale and duplicates

Where NMS fails: crowds

01Two people standing close have high-IoU boxes
02NMS keeps one, deletes the other
03Crowd counting undercounts
04Fixes: Soft-NMS (lower the score instead of deleting)
05or detectors with no NMS at all (Act 5)
Act 4 · Scale and duplicates · Day 2 · 51 / 121

2.51 · cards

This failure is why NMS-free detectors are such a big deal.

One look

What if we skip proposals and predict every box in one pass?

Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR · Day 2 · 54 / 121

2.54 · section

One-stage detectors trade a little accuracy for a lot of speed.

Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR

YOLO — You Only Look Once (2016)

YOLO — a one-stage detector: one forward pass of one network predicts all boxes and classes at once, with no separate proposal step.
Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR · Day 2 · 55 / 121

2.55 · definition

The name says it: one look, not two thousand.

Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR

The grid idea

  • Split the image into a 7 × 7 grid
  • The cell containing an object's centre is responsible for it
  • Each cell predicts boxes, a confidence for each, and class probabilities
Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR · Day 2 · 56 / 121

2.56 · diagram

Every cell is a tiny detector for its own region.

Worked example

YOLOv1's output — worked

  1. 7 × 7 grid
  2. 2 boxes per cell × (x, y, w, h, confidence) = 10 numbers
  3. + 20 class probabilities
  4. = 30 numbers per cell
  5. output tensor = 7 × 7 × 30
Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR · Day 2 · 57 / 121

2.57 · worked

The whole detection result is one tensor. That is why it is fast.

Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR

YOLO's loss in plain words

01Box errorhow far off are the box positions and sizes?
02Objectness errorwas "there is an object here" right?
03Class errorwas the class right?
04Total = weighted sum of the three
Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR · Day 2 · 58 / 121

2.58 · cards

Same multi-task idea as localising one object, but for every cell at once.

Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR

YOLOv1's limits

01Each cell predicts only 2 boxes → flocks of birds fail
02One class per cell
03Small objects get lost in coarse cells
04Boxes less precise than Faster R-CNN
Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR · Day 2 · 59 / 121

2.59 · cards

Every later YOLO version fixes one of these.

Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR

The YOLO evolution

v2anchors, batch norm
v3predictions at 3 scales (like FPN)
v4 / v5training tricks, heavy augmentation, easy tooling
v8anchor-free
YOLO26 (Jan 2026)end-to-end, no NMS step
Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR · Day 2 · 60 / 121

2.60 · table

(cut first) Don't memorise versions. Notice the direction: anchors in, then anchors out, then NMS out.

Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR

Anchor-based vs anchor-free

Anchor-based

  • adjust pre-defined template boxes
  • many hand-tuned settings

Anchor-free

  • predict the object centre and its distances to the box edges directly
  • simpler, fewer settings
Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR · Day 2 · 61 / 121

2.61 · compare

Modern detectors are mostly anchor-free.

Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR

DETR: detection as a set

  • Matched one-to-one to the ground truth during training
Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR · Day 2 · 62 / 121

2.62 · diagram

Each query learns to claim one object. Because training forbids two queries claiming the same object, duplicates never form.

Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR · Why DETR needs no NMS

NMS cleans up duplicates after the fact. DETR is trained so duplicates are never produced — no anchors, no NMS, one clean set of boxes.

Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR · Day 2 · 63 / 121

2.63 · rule

Day 3 explains the transformer inside. For today: one prediction per object, by design.

Act 5 · One look — YOLO and DETR

06

How good is the detector?

"It looks good on my photos" is not evaluation

Act 6 · How good is the detector? · Day 2 · 67 / 121

2.67 · section

This act is the most heavily tested on the exam. Go slowly.

Act 6 · How good is the detector?

When is a prediction correct?

01A prediction is a True Positive (TP) if
02its IoU with a ground-truth box ≥ threshold (e.g. 0.5)
03AND its class is correct
04AND that ground truth was not already matched
Act 6 · How good is the detector? · Day 2 · 68 / 121

2.68 · cards

All three conditions. The third one stops two predictions both counting for the same object.

Act 6 · How good is the detector?

TP, FP, FN for detection

True Positivea correct box on a real object
False Positivea box on nothing, wrong class, or a duplicate
False Negativea real object with no matching box
(True negatives are not counted — there are infinite empty boxes)
Act 6 · How good is the detector? · Day 2 · 69 / 121

2.69 · table

Detection has no true negatives. That is why we use precision and recall, not accuracy.

Act 6 · How good is the detector?

Precision and recall for detection

Precision = TP / (TP + FP)

  • "of the boxes I drew, how many were right?"

Recall = TP / (TP + FN)

  • "of the real objects, how many did I find?"
Act 6 · How good is the detector? · Day 2 · 70 / 121

2.70 · compare

Same definitions as Day 1, applied to boxes.

Act 6 · How good is the detector?

Which one matters more?

Airport weapon screening

  • missing one is a disaster → prioritise recall

Spam-like alerts to a busy operator

  • false alarms get ignored → prioritise precision
Act 6 · How good is the detector? · Day 2 · 71 / 121

2.71 · compare

The business decides which error is worse. Threshold Tycoon is exactly this.

Act 6 · How good is the detector? · Confidence changes everything

Raise the confidence threshold → fewer boxes → precision up, recall down. Lower it → more boxes → recall up, precision down.

Act 6 · How good is the detector? · Day 2 · 72 / 121

2.72 · rule

There is no single precision or recall for a detector, only one per threshold.

Act 6 · How good is the detector?

The precision–recall curve

  • Sort predictions by confidence
  • go down the list one by one
  • after each, compute precision and recall
  • plot recall on x, precision on y
  • A good detector stays high and to the right
Act 6 · How good is the detector? · Day 2 · 73 / 121

2.73 · diagram

The curve summarises every possible threshold at once.

Worked example

AP by hand — the setup

  1. 5 ground-truth objects
  2. 8 predictions sorted by confidence · TP · TP · FP · TP · FP · TP · FP · FP
Act 6 · How good is the detector? · Day 2 · 74 / 121

2.74 · worked

We already decided which are TP and which are FP using IoU ≥ 0.5. Now we build the curve.

Act 6 · How good is the detector?

AP by hand — the table

1 TPP 1/1 = 1.00R 1/5 = 0.2
2 TP2/2 = 1.000.4
3 FP2/3 = 0.670.4
4 TP3/4 = 0.750.6
5 FP3/5 = 0.600.6

Act 6 · How good is the detector? · Day 2 · 75 / 121

2.75 · table

Precision counts TPs so far divided by predictions so far. Recall counts TPs so far divided by 5. Recall never goes down.

Worked example

AP by hand — the area

  1. Interpolated precision at each recall = the best precision at that recall or higher
  2. R 0 → 0.4: 1.00
  3. R 0.4 → 0.6: 0.75
  4. R 0.6 → 0.8: 0.67
  5. R 0.8 → 1.0: 0 (one object never found)
  6. AP = 0.4×1.00 + 0.2×0.75 + 0.2×0.67 + 0.2×0 ≈ 0.68
Act 6 · How good is the detector? · Day 2 · 76 / 121

2.76 · worked

AP is the area under the cleaned-up curve. The last term is zero because recall never reached 1: one object was missed entirely.

Act 6 · How good is the detector?

From AP to mAP

mAP (mean Average Precision) — compute AP separately for each class, then take the mean. One number for the whole detector.

mAP@0.5 vs mAP@0.5:0.95

mAP@0.5

  • a hit needs IoU ≥ 0.5
  • forgiving

mAP@0.5:0.95

  • average of mAP at IoU 0.5, 0.55, … 0.95
  • rewards tight boxes
  • the COCO standard
  • always lower

Act 7 · Pixel-level understanding: segmentation

Semantic segmentation

Semantic segmentation — assigning a class label to every pixel in the image. The output is a label map the same size as the input.

A 512 by 512 image gives 262,144 classification decisions.

The obvious attempt: a sliding window per pixel

Idea

  • crop a patch around each pixel, classify the centre pixel

Problem

  • 262,144 crops per image, overlapping crops recompute the same features
  • absurdly slow

Without fully connected layers, the network outputs a map. But the map is tiny and blurry.

The tension

Downsampling

  • grows the receptive field
  • understands what

Full resolution

  • keeps fine detail
  • knows where

Segmentation needs both

Go down to understand, come back up to locate.

Encoder–decoder

The decoder must learn how to grow the map back.

Act 7 · Pixel-level understanding: segmentation

Upsampling options

01Nearest / bilinearcopy or average · no learning
02Unpoolingput values back in place
03Max unpoolingremember where the max came from
04Transposed convolutionlearned upsampling
Act 7 · Pixel-level understanding: segmentation · Day 2 · 90 / 121

2.90 · cards

Transposed convolution lets the network learn how to upsample.

Worked example

Transposed convolution — worked

  1. Input [1, 2]
  2. kernel [1, 1, 1] · stride 2
  3. Each input value stamps a scaled copy of the kernel, 2 steps apart
  4. 1 × [1, 1, 1] at positions 0–2
  5. 2 × [1, 1, 1] at positions 2–4
  6. overlaps add → output [1, 1, 3, 2, 2]
  7. length = (2 − 1)·2 + 3 = 5
Act 7 · Pixel-level understanding: segmentation · Day 2 · 91 / 121

2.91 · worked

(cut first) Formula: out = (in − 1)·S − 2P + K. Overlaps add up, which can create checkerboard artifacts.

Act 7 · Pixel-level understanding: segmentation · The problem with plain encoder–decoders

By the bottom of the encoder, the exact edges are gone. The decoder can guess the shape, but boundaries come out blurry.

Act 7 · Pixel-level understanding: segmentation · Day 2 · 92 / 121

2.92 · rule

Information destroyed by pooling cannot be recovered by upsampling alone.

Act 7 · Pixel-level understanding: segmentation

U-Net: skip connections across

  • Encoder levels are copied directly across to the matching decoder levels
  • The decoder gets both "what" (from below) and "where" (from the skip)
  • U-shaped diagram
Act 7 · Pixel-level understanding: segmentation · Day 2 · 93 / 121

2.93 · diagram

The encoder knows what, the decoder needs where, and skip connections deliver it. Different from ResNet's skips: these concatenate across the U.

Act 7 · Pixel-level understanding: segmentation

Why U-Net is everywhere

01Works with few training images
02Precise boundaries
03Medical imaging standard
04The core inside Stable Diffusion's denoiser (Day 3)

A detector says "3 people" in every frame. It cannot say whether they are the same 3 people, or count how many entered the shop today.

Detect, predict, match, update. Four verbs.

Act 8 · From frames to motion: tracking

Predict: a motion model

Motion model — a guess of where each tracked object will be in the next frame, based on its recent speed and direction. The Kalman filter is the classic way to do this.
Act 8 · From frames to motion: tracking · Day 2 · 104 / 121

2.104 · definition

If a car moved 10 pixels right each frame, expect it 10 pixels further right now.

Act 8 · From frames to motion: tracking

Match: who is who?

01Compute IoU between predicted track boxes and new detections
02High IoU = probably the same object
03Assign pairs so the total overlap is best (Hungarian algorithm)
04Optionally compare appearance too
Act 8 · From frames to motion: tracking · Day 2 · 105 / 121

2.105 · cards

IoU comes back. Matching is just IoU plus a fair assignment.

Act 8 · From frames to motion: tracking

Tracking failures

01ID switchtwo people cross and swap IDs
02Lost trackobject hidden behind a pillar, comes back with a new ID
03Fragmentationone object, many short tracks
Act 8 · From frames to motion: tracking · Day 2 · 106 / 121

2.106 · cards

ID switches ruin counts. They are the main thing tracking metrics punish.

Act 8 · From frames to motion: tracking

ByteTrack's idea

Old trackers

  • throw away low-confidence boxes before matching

ByteTrack

  • match high-confidence boxes first, then try the low-confidence ones against unmatched tracks
  • a half-hidden person keeps their ID
Act 8 · From frames to motion: tracking · Day 2 · 107 / 121

2.107 · compare

A low score often means partly hidden, not "not a person". ByteTrack keeps those boxes useful.

Act 8 · From frames to motion: tracking

Counting with a line

  • Draw a virtual line across the road
  • When a tracked object's centre crosses it → count in or out
  • Needs tracker IDs, otherwise one car is counted many times

Close of Day 2

Day 2 recap

  • Choose the simplest task that answers the question
  • IoU measures box overlap
  • Two-stage: propose then classify
  • FPN handles scale, NMS removes duplicates
  • YOLO looks once; DETR avoids duplicates by design
  • mAP summarises precision across recall and classes
  • U-Net brings "where" back with skip connections
  • Tracking = detect, predict, match, update
